stimuli.title: Saving the Scenery: How America Built Its National Parks
stimuli.source: Original passage written for KCE GED Prep. Quotations from the Yellowstone Act (1872), the Yosemite Grant (1864), the Antiquities Act (1906), and the National Park Service Organic Act (1916) are from public U.S. laws.
stimuli.html:
[1] On March 1, 1872, President Ulysses S. Grant signed a law setting aside more than two million acres of land in the Wyoming and Montana territories “as a public park or pleasuring-ground for the benefit and enjoyment of the people.” Yellowstone became the first national park in the world. The idea that a government should keep a vast landscape out of private hands, not for mining or timber but simply so that ordinary people could see it, was new. Over the next century and a half, it would spread to countries around the globe.

[2] Yellowstone was not the first time Congress had protected a landscape, however. Eight years earlier, in the middle of the Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln had signed the Yosemite Grant, which gave Yosemite Valley and a nearby grove of giant sequoias to the state of California on the condition that the land be held “for public use, resort, and recreation.” Because Yosemite was handed to a state rather than kept by the national government, historians usually call Yellowstone the first true national park. Still, the Yosemite Grant established the principle that some places were too remarkable to be sold.

[3] Setting land aside proved easier than protecting it. Congress gave Yellowstone almost no money, and its early superintendents could do little to stop poachers who killed elk and bison, or visitors who chipped souvenirs from the mineral formations around the geysers. In 1886, the U.S. Army was sent to manage the park, and soldiers patrolled it for more than three decades. Meanwhile, Congress created more parks, including Sequoia and Yosemite in 1890 and Mount Rainier in 1899. In 1906, the Antiquities Act gave presidents the power to protect “historic landmarks, historic and prehistoric structures, and other objects of historic or scientific interest” on federal land without waiting for Congress. President Theodore Roosevelt used it that same year to make Devils Tower in Wyoming the first national monument. But each park was run separately, with no shared rules and no trained staff.

[4] A battle in California exposed the weakness of this patchwork. Hetch Hetchy Valley, inside Yosemite National Park, was a granite valley that the naturalist John Muir compared to Yosemite Valley itself. The fast-growing city of San Francisco wanted to dam the valley's river for drinking water. Muir and his allies fought the plan for years, arguing that if one national park could be flooded, no park was truly safe. They lost: in 1913, Congress approved the dam. The defeat convinced park supporters that the parks needed an agency of their own, one whose main job would be to defend them.

[5] That agency arrived on August 25, 1916, when President Woodrow Wilson signed the law creating the National Park Service. The law gave the new service a two-part mission: “to conserve the scenery and the natural and historic objects and the wild life therein and to provide for the enjoyment of the same in such manner and by such means as will leave them unimpaired for the enjoyment of future generations.” The two halves of that sentence pull in different directions. Every road, campground, and hotel makes a park easier to enjoy, and every one also changes the land it sits on. Park managers have argued over where to draw that line ever since.

[6] The service's first director, Stephen Mather, a wealthy businessman, believed that the parks would survive only if Americans loved them, so he welcomed roads and railroads that brought tourists in. Later generations built on his approach. During the Great Depression, young men in the Civilian Conservation Corps built trails, shelters, and campgrounds in parks across the country. After World War II, as families took to the highways, a ten-year program called Mission 66 added more than one hundred visitor centers.

[7] The story of the parks also includes people who lost their homes to them. Many park lands had been hunting grounds, farmland, or sacred sites for Native nations long before explorers “discovered” them, and tribes were often pushed out when the parks were created. In recent decades, the Park Service has begun working with tribes to manage some lands together and to tell visitors a fuller history.

[8] Today the National Park System includes more than 400 sites, from geysers and glaciers to battlefields, seashores, and the childhood homes of presidents, and it records more than 300 million visits in a typical recent year. The tension written into the 1916 law has not gone away. Crowded roads, wildfire, and a changing climate all test the promise to keep the parks “unimpaired.” Whether that promise is kept depends, as Mather understood, on whether the public cares enough to keep it.

stimuli.title: Frost Watch
stimuli.source: Original fiction written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] The forecast on the kitchen radio called for twenty-six degrees by four in the morning. Grandpa Walt listened to it the way he listened to car salesmen, with his arms folded. “Twenty-six means twenty-four down in the low rows,” he said. “Get your boots.”

[2] Nora had planned to spend the evening on the phone with Jess, comparing housing forms for the university upstate, where they would both start in the fall. Instead she pulled on two sweatshirts and followed him out to the pump house, where the diesel engine coughed twice and then caught with a roar that rattled the tin walls.

[3] Within minutes, water was hissing from the little sprinklers at the base of every tree, eighty acres of them, row after row of dark shapes under a sky so clear it looked brittle. Nora knew the science; she had written a report on it in ninth grade. When water freezes, it gives off heat. As long as the sprinklers kept running, the ice forming on the trunks and branches would hold them near thirty-two degrees, even if the air dropped lower. Shut the water off too soon, and the wet trees would cool faster than if they had never been sprayed at all.

[4] Knowing the science did not make her any warmer. Grandpa walked the rows with a flashlight, checking each sprinkler head. When he found one clogged with sand, he knelt in the mud and cleared it with his pocketknife, as tenderly as if he were cleaning a child's scraped knee.

[5] “Dad says you got an offer,” Nora said around two o'clock. They were sitting on the tailgate of the truck with a thermos of coffee between them. “From the developer.”

[6] “I've had offers since your grandmother was alive.” He poured coffee into the thermos cap and handed it to her. “This one's bigger.”

[7] “Are you going to take it?”

[8] He didn't answer right away. Out in the dark, a sprinkler ticked around and around like a clock that couldn't decide what time it was. “My father planted the first forty acres with a mule and a shovel,” he said finally. “He used to say a grove is a promise you make to people you'll never meet.” He shrugged. “Then again, he never had to pay for fertilizer at today's prices.”

[9] Nora laughed, but the laugh came out thinner than she meant it to. She had spent most of her senior year counting the days until she could leave. She had never once imagined coming home to find the grove gone, a grid of rooftops where the trees had been.

[10] By five, the thermometer on the truck's mirror read twenty-three. Every tree wore a coat of ice. The leaves were sealed in glass, and the oranges hung inside clear shells, glowing whenever the flashlight passed over them. It was the strangest, most beautiful thing Nora had ever seen, and she was surprised to find her throat tight.

[11] The sun came up red behind the windbreak pines, and slowly the ice began to drip. Grandpa checked the thermometer, then held out the keys to the pump house.

[12] “Your call,” he said.

[13] “Me? I don't know when to—”

[14] “Sure you do. You wrote the report.”

[15] She waited until the thermometer climbed past thirty-four and the ice on the nearest branch slid loose and shattered at her feet. Then she shut down the engine. In the sudden quiet, she could hear the whole grove dripping, a soft, steady sound like rain that had decided to stay.

[16] “Well,” Grandpa said, looking down the long rows. “Looks like we kept another one.”

[17] Nora didn't ask whether he meant the crop or something else. She slipped her phone into her pocket without checking it and followed him down the first row, asking which trees his father had planted.

stimuli.title: Uniforms Free Students to Focus on Learning
stimuli.source: By Gloria Whitfield, middle school principal. Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
When Brookhaven Middle School adopted uniforms four years ago, many parents expected a fight. Instead, the policy has become one of the most popular changes our school has made. Requiring uniforms in public schools is a simple, affordable step that reduces conflict, improves safety, and lets students focus on learning.

The most immediate change was in our main office. In the year before uniforms, our staff handled 214 dress-code referrals, each one pulling a student out of class while adults debated the length of a skirt or the message on a T-shirt. In the first full year with uniforms, that number fell to 23. Our teachers estimate that they regained hours of instruction that had been lost to arguments over clothing.

Uniforms also take pressure off families. Before our policy, students regularly told counselors they were teased for wearing the same outfits or the “wrong” brands. When we surveyed our families after the switch, 68 percent said they were spending less on school clothing, and the average reported savings was about $150 per child per year. For families who cannot afford even basic uniform items, our parent association runs a clothing closet that provides them free of charge, so no child is left out.

Safety matters, too. When everyone on campus wears navy and khaki, staff can spot a visitor who does not belong within seconds. During a field trip to a crowded museum last spring, our chaperones could find every one of our students at a glance.

Our attendance rate also rose, from 91 percent to 94 percent, in the years after uniforms arrived. I believe students simply feel a stronger sense of belonging when they look like part of a team.

Critics claim that uniforms crush self-expression. But students at Brookhaven still express themselves through their art, their writing, their clubs, and their ideas, which is where self-expression belongs at school. A polo shirt does not silence anyone.

We ask students to dress for the work they do, just as hospitals, airlines, and sports teams do. Uniforms are not a cure-all, but they remove one daily distraction from young people who already have enough on their minds. Every public school should require them.

stimuli.title: Uniform Rules Miss the Real Problems in Our Schools
stimuli.source: By Darnell Price, parent and former school board member. Original passage written for KCE GED Prep. The quotation is from the U.S. Supreme Court opinion in Tinker v. Des Moines (1969).
stimuli.html:
Every few years, someone proposes school uniforms as the answer to whatever is troubling our schools. The idea is appealing because it is visible and easy to announce. But requiring uniforms in public schools costs families money, restricts students' rights, and does little to improve learning.

Start with cost. Supporters like to say uniforms save money, but families still have to buy regular clothes for evenings, weekends, and summer. In our district, a basic set of five uniform shirts and three pairs of pants from the approved vendor costs about $140 per child, and most children need a new set every year as they grow. For a family with three children, that is a $420 bill each August, on top of school supplies. Donation closets help, but students who rely on them often know it, and so do their classmates.

Next, consider the research. Researchers who examined national data on thousands of tenth graders found that students in schools with uniform policies showed no improvement in attendance, behavior, or test scores compared with similar students in schools without them. When a single school's numbers improve after it adopts uniforms, the school has usually changed other things at the same time, such as its leadership, its discipline rules, or its programs.

Uniform rules also raise questions about rights. In Tinker v. Des Moines (1969), the Supreme Court stated that students do not “shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate.” Clothing is one of the few ways a teenager can say who they are without saying a word. Some families also object to uniforms on religious or cultural grounds and end up in long disputes over exemptions.

Finally, uniforms can create the very problems they promise to solve. My daughter's friend was sent to the office three times in one month because her shirt was the wrong shade of blue. Once schools have uniforms, they start policing them, and that wastes the class time supporters claim to save. Before long, schools will be measuring the color of students' socks.

If we want safer, calmer schools, we should spend our time and money on counselors, mentoring, and smaller classes. Those are the investments that change how students feel about school. A required polo shirt is not.

stimuli.title: The Hidden Garden: The Microbes That Live With Us
stimuli.source: Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] Your body is never entirely your own. On your skin, in your mouth, and above all in your intestines live trillions of bacteria, along with smaller numbers of fungi, viruses, and other microscopic organisms. Scientists call this community the human microbiome. For most of the twentieth century, doctors thought of microbes mainly as germs to be destroyed. In 2007, the National Institutes of Health launched the Human Microbiome Project to identify the organisms that live in healthy people, and since then researchers have increasingly come to see the microbiome as something closer to an organ, one that helps keep its host healthy.

[2] For years, textbooks claimed that microbial cells in the body outnumbered human cells ten to one. That figure, it turns out, was based on a rough estimate made in the 1970s that no one had carefully checked. In 2016, a team of researchers recalculated using better data on cell sizes and body volume. They concluded that a typical adult carries about 38 trillion bacterial cells and about 30 trillion human cells, a ratio closer to one to one. The correction did not make the microbiome less important. It was a reminder that even widely repeated facts deserve a second look.

[3] Most of the body's bacteria live in the large intestine, where they do work the body cannot do alone. Human digestive enzymes cannot break down many of the fibers found in beans, whole grains, and vegetables. Gut bacteria can. As they ferment this fiber, they release substances called short-chain fatty acids, which help nourish the cells lining the colon. Gut bacteria also make vitamin K and several B vitamins, and they help train the immune system to tell the difference between harmless visitors and real threats. Perhaps most important, a crowded, well-established community of helpful bacteria leaves little room or food for harmful ones to take hold.

[4] That last benefit becomes clear when the community is disrupted. Antibiotics save millions of lives, but they kill helpful bacteria along with harmful ones. After a course of antibiotics, a bacterium called Clostridioides difficile can sometimes multiply in the emptied gut, causing severe diarrhea that may return again and again. For patients with repeated infections, doctors have had striking success with an unusual treatment: transferring stool from a healthy donor, which restores a diverse bacterial community. In clinical trials, this treatment has cured most patients whose infections kept returning after antibiotics alone.

[5] A person's microbiome begins forming at birth. Babies born vaginally pick up many of their first bacteria from their mothers during delivery, while babies born by cesarean section are colonized at first by more bacteria from skin and the hospital environment. Over the first few years of life, diet, siblings, pets, and surroundings all shape which species settle in. By adulthood, each person's microbiome is nearly as individual as a fingerprint, and it can still shift when diet changes.

[6] Researchers have found links between the makeup of the gut microbiome and conditions such as obesity, type 2 diabetes, inflammatory bowel disease, and even depression. These findings have generated enormous excitement, and stores now sell shelves of probiotic pills and drinks that promise to improve gut health. Scientists urge caution, however. Most of the links found so far are correlations: people with a certain condition tend to have a certain mix of bacteria, but that does not show whether the bacteria cause the condition, result from it, or are both caused by something else, such as diet. And while some probiotics have helped in specific situations, there is little evidence that the average healthy person benefits from taking them.

[7] For now, the best-supported advice is also the least exciting. A varied diet rich in fiber from plants feeds a varied community of microbes. Antibiotics should be taken when they are truly needed, and not otherwise. Beyond that, the microbiome remains one of the most active frontiers in medicine, a hidden garden that scientists are only beginning to map.

stimuli.title: A Closer Look: A Six-Week Fiber Study
stimuli.source: Original document written for KCE GED Prep. The study described is a hypothetical example.
stimuli.html:
A team of researchers recruited 40 healthy adults for a six-week study. Each volunteer chose one of two groups. Group A (20 people) increased their fiber intake by eating more beans, whole grains, fruits, and vegetables. Group B (20 people) kept eating their usual diets. At the start and end of the study, the researchers measured each volunteer's gut bacteria and gave it a diversity score, which reflects how many different kinds of bacteria are present. Higher scores mean greater diversity. Volunteers also reported whether they had felt bloated during the first week and the last week of the study.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: Yellowstone deserves to be called the first national park because Congress protected it before any other American land.
John Muir's defeat at Hetch Hetchy settled the conflict over how the national parks should be used.
The national parks grew from a new idea into a large system shaped by an ongoing struggle to protect the land while opening it to the public.
The National Park Service has harmed the parks by building too many roads and visitor centers.
items.explain:
The passage traces the parks from Yellowstone in 1872 (paragraph 1) to “more than 400 sites” today (paragraph 8). Along the way it returns again and again to one tension: the 1916 law's two goals “pull in different directions” (paragraph 5), and that tension “has not gone away” (paragraph 8).

Paragraph 2 says Congress protected Yosemite before Yellowstone, so the first choice is wrong. Muir's loss led to a new agency; it did not settle the conflict, which continues. The author describes road and visitor-center building but never says it harmed the parks.

items.prompt: In paragraph 5, the 1916 law calls for leaving the parks “unimpaired for the enjoyment of future generations.” As used here, unimpaired most nearly means
options: not damaged or weakened
not visited by people
not owned by any state
not yet explored
items.explain:
The law asks the service to “conserve the scenery” and to let people enjoy the parks in a way that will leave them in good condition for “future generations.” Impaired means damaged or weakened, so unimpaired means not damaged or weakened.

The same sentence calls for “enjoyment” by visitors, so “not visited by people” contradicts it. Ownership and exploration are not the subject of the sentence.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of paragraph 2?
options: to argue that Yosemite, not Yellowstone, should be called the first national park
to show that an earlier law set an important example while explaining why Yellowstone is still considered the first national park
to describe how the Civil War slowed the creation of national parks
to compare the scenery of Yosemite Valley with the scenery of Yellowstone
items.explain:
Paragraph 2 qualifies the claim in paragraph 1. It explains that the 1864 Yosemite Grant came first but went to a state, which is why “historians usually call Yellowstone the first true national park.” It then adds that the grant “established the principle that some places were too remarkable to be sold.”

The paragraph does not argue that Yosemite should get the title; it explains why it does not. It mentions the Civil War only to date the grant, and it does not compare scenery.

items.prompt: Based on the passage, put these events in the order in which they happened. Drag each event into the correct position.
choices: Congress approves a dam in Hetch Hetchy Valley.
President Lincoln signs the Yosemite Grant.
The National Park Service is created.
The U.S. Army is sent to manage Yellowstone.
Devils Tower becomes the first national monument.
items.explain: The passage gives a date for each event: the Yosemite Grant came “eight years earlier” than 1872, in 1864 (paragraph 2); the Army went to Yellowstone in 1886 (paragraph 3); Devils Tower became a national monument in 1906 (paragraph 3); Congress approved the Hetch Hetchy dam in 1913 (paragraph 4); and the National Park Service was created in 1916 (paragraph 5).

items.prompt: Paragraph 5 is shown below. Click the sentence in which the author directly states that the two goals of the 1916 law conflict with each other.
spans: That agency arrived on August 25, 1916, when President Woodrow Wilson signed the law creating the National Park Service.

The law gave the new service a two-part mission: “to conserve the scenery and the natural and historic objects and the wild life therein and to provide for the enjoyment of the same in such manner and by such means as will leave them unimpaired for the enjoyment of future generations.”
The two halves of that sentence pull in different directions.
Every road, campground, and hotel makes a park easier to enjoy, and every one also changes the land it sits on.
Park managers have argued over where to draw that line ever since.
items.explain:
“The two halves of that sentence pull in different directions” is the author's direct statement that the law's goals (conserving the land and providing for enjoyment) conflict.

The sentence about roads, campgrounds, and hotels gives an example of the conflict, and the last sentence describes its result. The second sentence quotes the law without commenting on it.

items.prompt: Based on paragraph 3, why was the U.S. Army most likely sent to manage Yellowstone in 1886?
options: Congress expected Yellowstone to be attacked by a foreign army.
Soldiers were needed to build roads and hotels for the growing number of tourists.
The park's superintendents asked to be replaced by trained park rangers.
The park's civilian managers lacked the money and power to stop people from damaging it.
items.explain:
Paragraph 3 opens, “Setting land aside proved easier than protecting it,” and explains that Congress gave Yellowstone “almost no money” and that superintendents “could do little to stop poachers” and souvenir hunters. The very next sentence says the Army was sent and “patrolled” the park. The logical inference is that soldiers were needed to stop the damage.

Nothing in the passage mentions a foreign threat, road building by soldiers, or a request from the superintendents. Trained rangers did not exist yet; the paragraph ends by noting there was “no trained staff.”

items.prompt: The final sentence of the passage mentions Stephen Mather mainly to
options: suggest that his belief that the parks depend on public support still applies today
criticize him for bringing too many tourists into the parks
show that he wrote the 1916 law that created the National Park Service
explain why he was chosen as the service's first director
items.explain:
Paragraph 6 says Mather “believed that the parks would survive only if Americans loved them.” The final sentence says the promise to protect the parks depends, “as Mather understood, on whether the public cares enough to keep it.” The author brings Mather back to show that his idea is still relevant to the parks' current challenges.

The author never criticizes Mather; crowded roads are listed as a modern problem, not blamed on him. The passage says President Wilson signed the law, and it never explains why Mather was chosen.

items.prompt: How is the fight over Hetch Hetchy Valley related to the creation of the National Park Service?
options: The National Park Service approved the dam in order to supply San Francisco with water.
John Muir's victory at Hetch Hetchy proved that the existing parks were already well protected.
The loss of Hetch Hetchy helped persuade park supporters that the parks needed an agency of their own.
The Hetch Hetchy dam was built to provide electricity for new visitor centers in Yosemite.
items.explain:
Paragraph 4 says Congress approved the dam in 1913 and that “the defeat convinced park supporters that the parks needed an agency of their own.” Paragraph 5 then begins, “That agency arrived” in 1916. The loss was a cause of the new agency.

The National Park Service did not exist in 1913, so it could not have approved the dam. Muir lost the fight rather than winning it, and the dam was for “drinking water,” not electricity for visitor centers.

items.prompt: In paragraph 1, Grandpa Walt listens to the forecast “the way he listened to car salesmen, with his arms folded.” This comparison suggests that he
options: finds the radio forecast entertaining
suspects the forecast is too hopeful about how cold it will get
plans to buy a new radio soon
believes the freeze will not reach the grove
items.explain:
People often listen to car salesmen with suspicion, and folded arms suggest doubt. Grandpa's next words confirm it: “Twenty-six means twenty-four down in the low rows.” He thinks it will be colder than the forecast says.

He does not treat the forecast as entertainment, and he clearly expects the freeze to reach the grove, since he immediately says, “Get your boots.” The radio itself is never the point.

items.prompt: In paragraph 4, Grandpa clears a clogged sprinkler “as tenderly as if he were cleaning a child's scraped knee.” What does this comparison show?
options: Grandpa is worried that Nora will get hurt in the dark.
Grandpa is clumsy and slow with his hands.
The sprinkler heads are delicate and expensive to replace.
Grandpa cares for the trees the way a person cares for family.
items.explain:
The simile compares Grandpa's work on a sprinkler to comforting a hurt child. Kneeling “in the mud” to do it “tenderly” shows that he treats the grove with the kind of love usually reserved for family, which prepares readers for his reluctance to sell.

The comparison is about how gently he works, not about danger to Nora, clumsiness, or the cost of the parts.

items.prompt: Why does Grandpa most likely hand Nora the keys to the pump house and say, “Your call”?
options: He wants to show that he trusts Nora to make an important decision about the grove.
He is too tired after the long night to walk to the pump house himself.
He has decided to sell the grove and no longer cares when the water is shut off.
He wants to find out whether Nora remembered her report so that she will choose to study science.
items.explain:
Paragraph 3 explains that shutting the water off too soon could damage the trees, so deciding when to stop is a serious responsibility. When Nora hesitates, Grandpa answers, “Sure you do,” showing confidence in her. Handing her the keys is a way of trusting her with the grove, the same thing his father passed down to him.

Nothing suggests he is too tired; he walks the rows afterward. His closing words, “we kept another one,” show he still cares about the grove. He mentions the report to reassure her, not to steer her toward a career.

items.prompt: Paragraph 9 is shown below. Click the sentence that reveals how eager Nora had been to get away from home.
spans: Nora laughed, but the laugh came out thinner than she meant it to.
She had spent most of her senior year counting the days until she could leave.
She had never once imagined coming home to find the grove gone, a grid of rooftops where the trees had been.
items.explain:
“Counting the days until she could leave” shows that Nora had been looking forward to leaving home for most of the year.

The first sentence shows her unease about the offer, and the last sentence shows that she had not thought about losing the grove. Neither describes her eagerness to leave.

items.prompt: Which details from the story best support the idea that Grandpa is deeply attached to the grove? Select two answers.
options: He listens to the radio forecast with his arms folded.
He kneels in the mud to clear a clogged sprinkler with his pocketknife.
He pours coffee into the thermos cap and hands it to Nora.
He repeats his father's saying that a grove is a promise you make to people you'll never meet.
He jokes that his father never had to pay today's prices for fertilizer.
He checks the thermometer on the truck's mirror at sunrise.
items.explain:
Kneeling in the mud to clear one sprinkler “tenderly” (paragraph 4) shows how much he cares for the trees. Repeating his father's saying (paragraph 8) shows that he sees the grove as a family promise that stretches across generations.

The folded arms show doubt about the forecast. Pouring coffee and checking the thermometer are routine actions. The joke about fertilizer prices actually points to the money pressure that might lead him to sell.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses a theme of the story?
options: Young people owe it to their families to give up their own plans.
Scientific knowledge matters more than experience passed down through families.
Caring for something through hard times can deepen a person's attachment to it.
In difficult times, money is more important than memories.
items.explain:
Nora starts the night thinking about leaving for college. After working through the freeze, she is moved by the ice-covered grove (paragraph 10), makes the call to shut off the water (paragraph 15), and ends by asking “which trees his father had planted” (paragraph 17). Caring for the grove through one hard night has deepened her connection to it.

The story never says Nora must give up college. Her science and Grandpa's experience work together rather than competing. Grandpa mentions money, but the story ends with the grove “kept,” not sold.

items.skill: How a paragraph contributes to a story
items.prompt: How does paragraph 10 contribute to the development of the story?
options: It explains the scientific reason the sprinklers protect the fruit.
It shows the ice-covered grove stirring feelings in Nora that she did not expect.
It reveals that the freeze has destroyed most of the crop.
It describes Grandpa's worry that the temperature is falling too fast.
items.explain:
In paragraph 10, Nora sees the trees “sealed in glass” and calls it “the strangest, most beautiful thing” she has ever seen, and she is “surprised to find her throat tight.” This marks a turning point in her feelings about the grove.

The science is explained in paragraph 3, not paragraph 10. The ice is protecting the fruit, not destroying it; Grandpa later says “we kept another one.” Grandpa does not appear in paragraph 10.

items.prompt: In paragraph 17, Nora “didn't ask whether he meant the crop or something else.” This suggests that Grandpa's words “we kept another one” may also refer to
options: the money the family will earn from the developer's offer
the pump house engine, which nearly failed during the night
Nora's friendship with Jess
the family's bond with the grove, including Nora's
items.explain:
On the surface, “we kept another one” means they saved another year's crop. The narrator hints at “something else.” Throughout the night Nora has grown closer to the grove, and in the last sentence she asks about the trees her great-grandfather planted. The family's connection to the grove, which seemed at risk, has been “kept” as well, now including Nora.

Keeping the grove is the opposite of taking the developer's money. The engine never fails, and Jess is not part of what “we” kept.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the notice. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“We are writing to let you know about changes to your Everyday Checking account that will take {{0}} on November 1.”

options: affect
effect
affects
effecting

items.explain:
The phrase “take effect” uses the noun effect, meaning a result or the start of something's operation.

Affect is usually a verb meaning “to influence,” so it cannot follow “take” here. “Effecting” is a verb form and does not fit after “take.”

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the notice. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Beginning November 1, the monthly service fee for Everyday Checking {{0}} from $5 to $8.”

options: increased
had increased
will increase
increasing

items.explain:
The notice is dated September 15, and the change begins November 1, so the action is in the future: will increase.

“Increased” and “had increased” describe the past. “Increasing” cannot be the main verb of a sentence without a helping verb such as “is.”

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the notice. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“It will be waived for any month in which you keep a daily balance of at least $500, {{0}} at least one direct deposit, or are under the age of 25.”

options: receive
receiving
the receipt of
to receive

items.explain:
The three conditions share the subject “you”: you keep a balance, you receive a deposit, or you are under 25. To keep the list parallel, the middle item needs the same verb form: receive.

“Receiving,” “the receipt of,” and “to receive” each break the pattern of the other two items.

items.prompt:
Read these sentences from the notice. Choose the transition that best connects them.

“The overdraft fee will drop from $35 to $25, and we will charge no more than two overdraft fees per day. {{0}} we will no longer charge any fee when an account is overdrawn by $10 or less.”

options: Instead,
However,
As a result,
In addition,

items.explain:
Both sentences describe ways the overdraft rules are becoming friendlier to customers. The second sentence adds another benefit, so In addition, is correct.

“However” signals a contrast, but there is none. “Instead” suggests the new rule replaces the earlier ones, which it does not. “As a result” suggests the lower fee causes the $10 rule, which the notice does not say.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the notice. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Each of the new cards {{0}} a chip for added security.”

options: have
has
are having
having

items.explain:
The subject is Each, which is singular. The phrase “of the new cards” comes between the subject and the verb but does not change it. A singular subject takes the singular verb has.

“Have” agrees with “cards,” the word closest to the blank, which is the common mistake. “Are having” is plural and unnatural, and “having” cannot serve as the main verb.

items.prompt:
Read these sentences from the notice. Choose the option that correctly completes them.

“Our mobile app is also changing. {{0}} new design lets you lock a lost card with a single tap.”

options: It's
Their
Its
Its'

items.explain:
The design belongs to the app, so a possessive pronoun is needed. The possessive form of it is Its, with no apostrophe.

“It's” means “it is” (“It is new design” makes no sense). “Their” is plural, but “app” is singular. “Its'” is not a word.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the notice. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“If you suspect fraud, call us right away at 1-800-555-0142{{0}} representatives are available 24 hours a day.”

options: , our
our
. Our

items.explain:
“If you suspect fraud, call us right away at 1-800-555-0142” and “Our representatives are available 24 hours a day” are both complete sentences. Separating them with a period, . Our, is correct.

Joining them with only a comma creates a comma splice, and joining them with nothing creates a fused (run-on) sentence.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the notice. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Please note that all branches will be closed on November 11 in observance of {{0}}.”

options: veterans day
Veterans Day
Veterans day
veterans Day

items.explain:
The name of a holiday is a proper noun, so every main word is capitalized: Veterans Day.

The other choices leave one or both words lowercase.

items.prompt:
Read the closing of the notice. Choose the option that best completes it.

“We value your business. {{0}}”

options: Thank you for choosing Prairie Hollow Savings Bank.
Because you have chosen Prairie Hollow Savings Bank.
Thanking you for choosing Prairie Hollow Savings Bank.
For choosing Prairie Hollow Savings Bank.

items.explain:
Thank you for choosing Prairie Hollow Savings Bank. is a complete sentence (the subject “I” or “we” is understood in this common expression), and it closes the notice politely.

“Because you have chosen…” is a dependent clause with no main clause. “Thanking you for choosing…” and “For choosing…” are phrases with no main verb. All three are fragments.

essay.prompt:
The articles present arguments from a supporter and a critic of requiring students in public schools to wear uniforms.

In your response, analyze both positions presented in the articles to determine which one is best supported. Use relevant and specific evidence from both articles to support your response.

Type your response in the box. This task may require approximately 45 minutes to complete.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the email. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Your delivery crew {{0}} it to my home on June 10.”

options: delivers
delivered
has delivered
will deliver

items.explain:
The delivery happened on a specific past date, June 10, so the simple past tense delivered is correct.

“Has delivered” (present perfect) is not used with a specific past date. “Delivers” and “will deliver” are present and future.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the email. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“When I opened the box, I found that the door glass was cracked and one of the leveling feet {{0}} missing.”

options: were
are
was
have been

items.explain:
The subject of the clause is one, which is singular; “of the leveling feet” is a phrase that describes it. The sentence is in the past tense, so the correct verb is was.

“Were,” “are,” and “have been” are plural verbs that wrongly agree with “feet.” “Are” also shifts to the present tense.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the email. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“I called your service line that afternoon and waited on hold for more {{0}} forty minutes.”

options: then
than
that

items.explain:
Than is used to make comparisons (“more than forty minutes”).

Then refers to time (“first this, then that”), and “more that forty minutes” makes no sense.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the email. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“The representative who finally answered told my wife and {{0}} that a replacement would arrive within five business days.”

options: myself
I
mine
me

items.explain:
The pronoun is an object of the verb “told,” so it must be in the object case: me. Test it by removing “my wife and”: “told me,” not “told I.”

“Myself” is reflexive and is used only when the subject (here, the representative) is the same person. “Mine” is possessive.

items.prompt:
Read these sentences from the email. Choose the option that best completes them.

“That was more than two weeks ago. Since then, I have called three times. {{0}}”

options: Each time being told that the order is “in process.”
Which each time the answer was that the order is “in process.”
Each time, I have been told that the order is “in process.”
Each time told that the order is “in process.”

items.explain:
Each time, I have been told that the order is “in process.” has a subject (“I”) and a complete verb (“have been told”), so it is a full sentence. Its present perfect tense also matches “I have called.”

“Each time being told…” and “Each time told…” have no subject and complete verb. “Which each time…” is a dependent clause that cannot stand alone.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the email. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“My family of five now has three {{0}} worth of laundry piled up, and we have been paying to use a laundromat across town.”

options: weeks'
week's
weeks
weeks's

items.explain:
In expressions of time and value such as “a day's pay” or “three weeks' worth,” the time word is possessive. Because weeks is plural and ends in s, the apostrophe goes after the s: weeks'.

“Week's” is singular possessive, but there are three weeks. “Weeks” has no apostrophe, and “weeks's” is not a correct form.

items.prompt:
Read these sentences from the email. Choose the transition that best connects them.

“Please deliver a working replacement and remove the damaged machine by June 30. {{0}}, I will cancel the order and expect a full refund, including the $59 delivery fee.”

options: For example
Furthermore
Similarly
Otherwise

items.explain:
The second sentence tells what the writer will do if the request in the first sentence is not met. Otherwise means “if not,” which fits exactly.

“Furthermore” would add a second demand, which makes no sense because canceling and receiving a replacement cannot both happen. “For example” and “Similarly” do not fit the relationship.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the email. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“I would also like to speak with a manager {{0}} can explain what went wrong with my order.”

options: whom
which
who
whose

items.explain:
The pronoun is the subject of the verb “can explain” (the manager can explain), and it refers to a person, so who is correct.

“Whom” is used for objects (test: “he can explain,” not “him can explain”). “Which” refers to things, not people, and “whose” shows possession.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: The microbes that live in and on the body play important roles in health, though much about them is still uncertain.
Probiotic products are the most effective way to keep the microbiome healthy.
Antibiotics do more harm than good because they destroy helpful bacteria.
Scientists have proven that the makeup of the gut microbiome causes obesity and depression.
items.explain:
The passage describes what gut microbes do for the body (paragraph 3), what happens when they are disrupted (paragraph 4), and how the microbiome forms (paragraph 5). It also stresses uncertainty: most links to disease are “correlations” (paragraph 6), and scientists “are only beginning to map” the microbiome (paragraph 7).

The author says there is “little evidence” that probiotics help most healthy people, states that antibiotics “save millions of lives,” and says the disease links do not show cause.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of paragraph 2?
options: to prove that the microbiome is less important than scientists once believed
to explain how researchers count every cell in the human body
to correct a commonly repeated figure while showing that the microbiome still matters
to argue that textbooks should no longer be used to teach science
items.explain:
Paragraph 2 explains that the “ten to one” claim came from an unchecked estimate and that a 2016 recalculation found a ratio “closer to one to one.” It then adds, “The correction did not make the microbiome less important.”

That sentence directly rules out the first choice. The paragraph mentions better data but does not explain counting methods in detail, and it does not argue against textbooks.

items.prompt: In paragraph 5, babies born by cesarean section “are colonized at first by more bacteria from skin and the hospital environment.” As used here, colonized most nearly means
options: taken over by a foreign government
settled and lived in
protected from infection
sorted into groups
items.explain:
The paragraph is about which bacteria a baby “pick[s] up” first and which species “settle in.” Here colonized means that bacteria arrive and make their home in the baby's body: settled and lived in.

“Taken over by a foreign government” is the historical meaning of the word, which does not fit a sentence about bacteria. The sentence does not describe protection or sorting.

items.prompt: Sort each statement according to how the passage presents it. Drag each statement into the correct box.
choices: Gut bacteria help nourish the cells lining the colon.
Bacteria in the gut cause type 2 diabetes.
A typical adult carries roughly as many bacterial cells as human cells.
Probiotic products improve the health of most healthy people.
Stool transfers have cured most patients in trials whose infections kept returning after antibiotics.
bins: Presented as unproven or not supported
items.explain:
Supported: Paragraph 3 states that short-chain fatty acids from gut bacteria “help nourish the cells lining the colon.” Paragraph 2 reports the 2016 finding of a ratio “closer to one to one.” Paragraph 4 reports that stool transfers “cured most patients” in clinical trials.

Unproven or not supported: Paragraph 6 says the links to conditions such as diabetes are “correlations” that do not show whether bacteria “cause the condition.” It also says “there is little evidence that the average healthy person benefits” from probiotics.

items.prompt: Paragraph 6 is shown below. Click the sentence that explains why the links between the microbiome and disease do not prove that bacteria cause disease.
spans: Researchers have found links between the makeup of the gut microbiome and conditions such as obesity, type 2 diabetes, inflammatory bowel disease, and even depression.
These findings have generated enormous excitement, and stores now sell shelves of probiotic pills and drinks that promise to improve gut health.

Most of the links found so far are correlations: people with a certain condition tend to have a certain mix of bacteria, but that does not show whether the bacteria cause the condition, result from it, or are both caused by something else, such as diet.
And while some probiotics have helped in specific situations, there is little evidence that the average healthy person benefits from taking them.
items.explain:
The fourth sentence explains the problem: the links are “correlations,” and a correlation “does not show whether the bacteria cause the condition, result from it, or are both caused by something else.”

“Scientists urge caution, however” signals that a reason is coming but does not give it. The first sentence states the links, and the last sentence is about probiotics, not about cause and effect.

items.prompt: Based on paragraphs 3 and 4, why can Clostridioides difficile multiply after a person takes antibiotics?
options: Antibiotics are made from C. difficile.
C. difficile is a helpful bacterium that antibiotics make stronger.
Stool transfers introduce C. difficile into the gut.
Antibiotics wipe out many of the helpful bacteria that normally crowd out harmful ones.
items.explain:
Paragraph 3 says a “well-established community of helpful bacteria leaves little room or food for harmful ones.” Paragraph 4 says antibiotics “kill helpful bacteria along with harmful ones,” leaving an “emptied gut” where C. difficile can multiply. Putting these together, losing the helpful bacteria gives the harmful one room to grow.

The passage calls the infection “severe,” so C. difficile is not helpful. Stool transfers are the cure, not the cause.

items.prompt: Which details from the passage support the claim that a person's microbiome is shaped by his or her experiences and surroundings? Select two answers.
options: Babies born vaginally and babies born by cesarean section first pick up different bacteria.
Gut bacteria make vitamin K and several B vitamins.
An adult's microbiome can shift when his or her diet changes.
Human digestive enzymes cannot break down many plant fibers.
The ten-to-one figure was based on an unchecked estimate from the 1970s.
Researchers have linked the gut microbiome to depression.
items.explain:
Paragraph 5 shows that how a baby is born affects which bacteria arrive first, and that an adult microbiome “can still shift when diet changes.” Both show the microbiome being shaped by a person's experiences.

Vitamins and fiber digestion describe what bacteria do, not what shapes them. The ten-to-one figure is about counting cells. The link to depression is a correlation that does not show what shaped the microbiome.

items.prompt: In paragraph 1, the author says researchers now see the microbiome as “something closer to an organ.” The author uses this comparison mainly to emphasize that
options: the microbiome does work that helps keep the body healthy
the microbiome can be removed by surgery like other organs
microbes are made of human cells
doctors were right to treat all microbes as germs to be destroyed
items.explain:
Organs such as the heart or liver perform jobs the body needs. The same sentence describes the microbiome as something “that helps keep its host healthy,” and paragraph 3 lists its jobs: digesting fiber, making vitamins, and training the immune system.

The comparison is about function, not surgery. Paragraph 2 makes clear that bacterial cells and human cells are different. The comparison contrasts with the old view of microbes as germs; it does not support it.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the author's view of probiotic products?
options: The author is enthusiastic about them because stores sell so many kinds.
The author doubts that they help the average healthy person.
The author is certain that they cause harm.
The author is confident that they can treat depression.
items.explain:
Paragraph 6 says “there is little evidence that the average healthy person benefits from taking them,” and paragraph 7 calls a fiber-rich diet “the best-supported advice.” The author is doubtful about probiotics for healthy people.

The author mentions that stores sell many products only to show the excitement that scientists caution against. The author never says probiotics are harmful and even notes that some have “helped in specific situations.” The link to depression is described as an unproven correlation.

items.prompt: Which statement is supported by the data in the table?
options: Group A's average diversity score at the end of the study was about twice Group B's.
Group B's average diversity score went down during the study.
Group A's average diversity score rose 8 points more than Group B's.
The two groups' average diversity scores were more than 10 points apart at the start.
items.explain:
Group A rose from 62 to 71, an increase of 71 − 62 = 9 points. Group B rose from 61 to 62, an increase of 62 − 61 = 1 point. The difference is 9 − 1 = 8 points.

Final scores of 71 and 62 are nowhere near a two-to-one ratio. Group B's score went up, not down. The starting scores, 62 and 61, were only 1 point apart.

items.prompt: What percentage of the volunteers in Group A reported bloating during week 1?
items.explain:
In Group A, 9 of 20 volunteers reported bloating in week 1. 9 ÷ 20 = 0.45, which is 45%.

22.5% comes from dividing by all 40 volunteers (9 ÷ 40) instead of the 20 people in Group A. 9% treats the count as a percentage, and 90% comes from dividing by 10.

items.prompt: Which feature of the study most weakens the conclusion that eating more fiber caused the increase in Group A's diversity score?
options: The researchers measured diversity scores at both the start and the end of the study.
Group B kept eating its usual diet.
Both groups had the same number of volunteers.
Because volunteers chose their own groups, people in Group A may have differed from Group B in other ways, such as exercise or other eating habits.
items.explain:
The description says, “Each volunteer chose one of two groups.” People who choose a high-fiber diet may also exercise more or have other healthy habits, and those differences, not the fiber, could explain some of the change. Randomly assigning volunteers to groups would avoid this problem.

Measuring at the start and end, having an unchanged comparison group, and using equal group sizes are all strengths of the design, not weaknesses.

items.prompt: How do the study's results relate to the passage “The Hidden Garden”?
options: They are consistent with the passage's advice that a fiber-rich diet feeds a varied community of microbes.
They prove that eating more fiber cures conditions such as type 2 diabetes.
They contradict the passage's claim that the adult microbiome can change when diet changes.
They show that probiotic products work better than fiber.
items.explain:
Paragraph 7 of the passage says, “A varied diet rich in fiber from plants feeds a varied community of microbes.” In the study, the higher-fiber group's diversity score rose 9 points, compared with 1 point for the usual-diet group. The results fit the passage's advice.

The study did not measure any disease. Group A's change in diversity supports the passage's claim that an adult microbiome can shift with diet. The study did not test probiotics.
